title: Geopolitics Energy Transition: Climate & Security Nexus | World Economic Forum
author: Pim Valdre
text: In an uncertain world, leaders need to navigate the tensions created by the convergence between energy security, climate ambition and geopolitical developments. The energy and climate transition – globally and locally – is happening in an increasingly uncertain world. Conflicts and geopolitical instability in many regions, including in the Strait of Hormuz and Ukraine, are disrupting energy markets and infrastructure, and damaging energy infrastructure assets. From both a climate and energy perspective, this reality underscores a growing recognition that energy security, climate ambition and geopolitical developments cannot be treated as separate domains.Global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to decrease by 0.4% in 2026 – driven by the expansion of solar and wind power and the conflict in Iran. Despite the global turbulence and shocks partly explaining this decline, the energy transition itself is not standing still. Renewable technologies have become increasingly cost-competitive, while electrification is advancing across transport, buildings and industry, driving electricity demand faster than overall energy use and requiring major investments and upgrades in power infrastructure.Meanwhile, climate ambition is driven by different momentum, with market forces, economic opportunity and the need to reduce exposure to imported fossil fuels emerging as key factors.This creates a situation in which geopolitical shocks can have a dual effect. While they may in some cases accelerate efforts to diversify national energy sources and expand renewable energy production, they may also encourage countries to protect existing carbon-intensive industries in pursuit of greater energy security and self-sufficiency.Energy security as the strongest multiplier of climate actionFor many countries, renewables now represent more than an environmental and climate imperative. They offer the possibility of low-cost domestic energy production that can increase diversification, reduce exposure to international commodity markets and improve resilience.Accordingly, funding renewable generation, storage and grids represents a long-term investment that helps reduce dependence on fuel imports whose prices and availability are vulnerable to geopolitical events.Oil markets have also shown a resilience and flexibility few expected. While the oil shocks in the 1970s led to more diversification, energy efficiency and international cooperation, we may see countries and companies learning different lessons and taking divergent actions following the current shock.This is where climate action and industrial strategy increasingly intersect. For countries without large domestic fossil fuel reserves, moving towards clean energy and low-carbon production is not simply a response to climate change.Such a move is also a strategy for economic independence and competitiveness. The needs and opportunities for cost-effective solutions are particularly pronounced in many emerging economies where energy demand is rising fast, as these markets also often face a higher cost of capital than advanced economies. Climate finance, adaptation funding and support for loss and damage continue to fall short of what is required. In parallel, the gap between climate pledges made under the Paris Agreement and verifiable action has eroded trust.The answer will require stronger cooperation across governments, business, multilateral institutions and financial actors, as well as a broader understanding of cooperation itself.In a fragmented geopolitical environment, cooperation may not always mean complete alignment and a single-track approach to diplomacy and partnerships. It may instead involve practical collaborations and unconventional partnerships involving stakeholders across energy, climate and national security.Navigating the next phase of the energy transitionLeaders point towards a common objective across energy and climate stakeholders: moving from climate ambition to implementation. Conversations underscore a growing gap between ambition and delivery. However, some key insights could help inform how we manage these interdependencies:   Energy security can accelerate the transition – but does not guarantee it. Energy security has become a major concern for governments and business and a powerful driver for energy transition decisions. The disruption around the Strait of Hormuz exposed the risks of fossil-fuel dependence and strengthened the case for renewables and energy diversification. But oil markets have also shown considerable resilience, and some countries may opt for energy pragmatism, including scaling domestic carbon-intensive energy sources.The critical challenge is building systems that are resilient and competitive in this new era. Moving beyond deploying individual technologies, the challenge is about building the grids, local capabilities and resilient supply chains needed to connect all the elements. The recent World Economic Forum report, Enabling the Electricity Era, points to key actions needed to upgrade the electricity system to meet tomorrow’s energy needs, including unlocking hidden capacity and delivering essential infrastructure faster.The next major test lies beyond renewable power. Renewable electricity is advancing, but the harder transition is still ahead in key sectors of the global economy from mobility, fertilizers and mining to heavy industry. Solutions must extend beyond green electricity to include biofuels, hydrogen, carbon capture and circular economy models.Read moreThe contours of a new leadership agenda are being drawnIntegrating climate, energy, and geopolitics is not a matter of broadening the climate agenda for its own sake. It reflects the reality that these systems now shape one another.Energy and geopolitical shocks affect climate politics. Climate policies influence industrial competitiveness, while geopolitical competition affects the availability and cost of technologies. Nature, land and biodiversity are similarly connected to economic resilience, food systems and energy infrastructure, even though global governance often continues to treat them as separate issues.This creates a new leadership test. Leaders will need to move beyond defending individual agendas and focus on the connections between them and the tensions that have appeared because of growing interdependencies.International cooperation will also need to become more practical. Progress may not depend on every country following the same pathway, but on finding areas where cooperation delivers clear strategic value: resilient supply chains, grid development, technology deployment, investment, standards and capacity-building.The most important shift is therefore one of mindset. Climate action is not a separate project to be protected from geopolitical reality, and an accelerated energy transition is not a certain outcome of geopolitical events.Read more     Follow this topic.
